# Packaging the rounding check as a skill {#sec-workflow-rounding-skill}

::: callout-tip
A skill is a versioned folder of procedural knowledge that an agent loads when
a task calls for it. Packaging a check as a skill is what makes the check
outlive the person who wrote the prompt.
:::

@sec-workflow-rounding ended with a working check and a failing delivery
mechanism. The scan, the boundary test, and the triage rules produced a real
finding in `Merck/metalite`. All of them lived in the head of the reviewer who
ran the prompt. This chapter is the second turn of the same lifecycle loop,
with a different unit of work: not a prompt, but a package.

::: {.callout-note title="Maturity: Reproducible prototype (second cycle)"}
The skill in
[`examples/rounding/rounding-rule-review`](https://github.com/elong0527/ai4csr/tree/main/examples/rounding/rounding-rule-review)
is complete and runnable, and its results on the fixtures and on metalite are
reproducible. The automation triggers in the Deploy section are a design; no
scheduled job or CI workflow has been committed or run.
:::

| Example contract | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Problem** | A check that works once is not a workflow if its knowledge is not written down |
| **Learning objective** | Show how procedural knowledge, deterministic tools, and coverage reporting become a portable, versioned artifact |
| **Workflow boundary** | Begins with an accepted set of findings from the first cycle; ends with a skill that a colleague can run and a plan for triggering it |
| **Non-goals** | Build an agent platform, automate the human decision, or claim the skill is qualified for GxP use |
| **Why this is well defined** | The unit of work is a folder with a specification, and its correctness is measured on fixtures with known answers |

## Plan --- Frame the second cycle

The first cycle's monitoring output named four defects in the workflow, not in
metalite:

| Observed in cycle 1 | What the second cycle must provide |
|---|---|
| The catalog and triage rules lived in one person's memory | Written procedure that travels with the check |
| Nothing recorded what was scanned or under which rule version | A coverage statement on every run |
| The check ran when someone remembered | A defined trigger |
| The approved helper was discarded by hand on every run | A path to an allowlist |

### Canonical artifact: Workflow brief

- **Problem.** The detection logic is correct and unrepeatable.
- **Minimum valuable workflow.** A folder that any agent client can load, that
  states the procedure, ships the two scripts, and reports its own coverage.
- **Non-goals.** Automating the human decision, or expanding to rules 2 and 3
  in this cycle.
- **Success measures.** A colleague who has never seen the first cycle
  reproduces its metalite finding; the compliant fixture still produces no
  finding; every run states which rules it did not check.
- **Why not just a longer prompt.** A prompt is retyped, drifts, and cannot be
  versioned or reviewed. The same text in a file has an owner and a history.

## Design --- Specify the skill

### What a skill is

An **agent skill** is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` file with metadata
and instructions, plus optional scripts, references, and assets. The format is
defined by the
[Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification) and is
supported across several agent clients, which is what makes the folder
portable rather than tied to one vendor.

The design principle behind the format is **progressive disclosure**. An agent
loads material in three stages, so a skill can be detailed without consuming
context until it is needed:

| Stage | What loads | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Discovery | `name` and `description` only, for every installed skill | About 100 tokens each |
| Activation | The full `SKILL.md` body, once the skill is selected | Under 5000 tokens recommended |
| Execution | Files under `references/`, `scripts/`, `assets/`, on demand | Only what is read |

For a Biometrics team, the practical consequence is that the rule contract can
be long and precise. It is a `references/` file, read only when a finding needs
it, not text competing for room in every conversation.

### Frontmatter is the contract with the agent

`SKILL.md` begins with YAML frontmatter:

| Field | Required | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | Yes | Up to 64 characters, lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens, matching the directory name |
| `description` | Yes | Up to 1024 characters, stating what the skill does **and when to use it** |
| `license` | No | License name or bundled file |
| `compatibility` | No | Environment requirements, such as required executables |
| `metadata` | No | Arbitrary string keys, used here for the version and rule-contract identifier |
| `allowed-tools` | No | Pre-approved tools. Experimental, and support varies |

The `description` is the only part an agent sees before deciding to activate
the skill, so it carries the trigger vocabulary a reviewer would actually use:

```yaml
name: rounding-rule-review
description: Reviews R source code for violations of business rule
  BR-NUM-001.1, which requires exact decimal ties to round half away from zero.
  Scans for rounding sites including formatting functions such as formatC,
  sprintf, and format, proves tie behavior with a boundary test, and drafts a
  GitHub issue reporting confirmed findings. Use when asked to verify rounding
  conventions, check half away from zero, audit display precision, or review an
  R package for rounding compliance.
compatibility: Requires Rscript on PATH and read access to the R source being
  reviewed. Issue creation requires the gh CLI.
metadata:
  version: "1.0"
  rule-contract: BR-NUM-001 v1.0
```

Naming the rule contract version in `metadata` is what allows two runs months
apart to be compared. A finding is only interpretable against the rule that
produced it.

### Canonical artifact: Task contract, revised

The objective and boundaries are unchanged from @sec-workflow-rounding. Three
elements change:

| Element | Cycle 1 | Cycle 2 |
|---|---|---|
| **Procedure** | In the reviewer's head | `SKILL.md`, versioned |
| **Trigger** | A person remembers | On demand, and a designed schedule |
| **Required output** | Findings and probe output | Also an explicit statement of rules **not** checked |

## Build --- The skill package

```
rounding-rule-review/
  SKILL.md                      Metadata and the four-step procedure
  references/
    rounding-rules.md           BR-NUM-001 v1.0, the rule contract
  scripts/
    scan-rounding-sites.R       Catalog scan for candidate rounding sites
    probe-tie-behavior.R        Boundary test, returns PASS or FAIL
  assets/
    issue-template.md           Structure of a reported finding
```

The procedure in `SKILL.md` is the first cycle's tacit knowledge written down.
Three passages carry most of its value.

**The instruction that prevents the false clean report.**

> Do not substitute a plain search for `round(`. A rounding site is any call
> that can change a reported value at an exact decimal tie, and formatting
> functions round as a side effect of display.

**The instruction that prevents a confident wrong explanation.** The skill
tells the agent that `formatC()` diverges for two different reasons, tie mode
and binary representation, and then constrains the claim:

> Report the observed divergence and its frequency at the boundary values. Do
> not claim the function "uses banker's rounding" as a blanket explanation.

**The instruction that keeps the human in the decision.**

> By default, render the issue body to a file and stop. Create a real GitHub
> issue only when the user explicitly asks for one, and show the body first.

A prompt that omits this last line will eventually post something. The default
belongs in the artifact, not in the reviewer's discipline.

### Try it yourself

The prompt in @sec-workflow-rounding can be run again with one change: add the
sentence the rule contract supplies. Send this to
[arena.ai](https://arena.ai/agent) and compare the two answers.

``` text
Review the R source of the metalite package at the commit linked below and
verify whether it follows the business rule that exact decimal ties are rounded
half away from zero, as SAS ROUND() does and as cards::round5() implements.

A rounding site is any call that can change a reported value at an exact
decimal tie. Formatting functions round as a side effect of display, so
formatC(), sprintf(), and format() are rounding sites. A package that never
calls round() can still violate this rule.

Report every rounding site with file and line numbers, and show the evidence
for how each one behaves at an exact tie. Report separately any site you
examined and discarded, with the reason. State which parts of the source you
did not check.

Repository at a fixed commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef

R source directory at that commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef/R

Do not propose a code change. Do not modify any repository.
```

The added paragraph is not a better-worded instruction. It is a quotation from
a versioned document with an owner, a change history, and an approval path.
That is the entire difference between the two runs, and it is the reason the
knowledge belongs in `references/rounding-rules.md` rather than in whatever a
reviewer happens to type.

Two honest qualifications. A single pair of runs is a demonstration, not a
benchmark; the measured comparison is the fixture table later in this chapter.
And as in the first cycle, the agent cannot create a GitHub issue in this
setting.

### Write down what the skill cannot do

`SKILL.md` ends with its own limitations: the scanner is line based, so a call
split across lines is reported at its first line and a dynamically constructed
call is not detected; there is no allowlist, so the organization's own approved
helper is reported as a candidate every run; and only rule BR-NUM-001.1 is
covered.

Stating limitations inside the artifact, rather than in a chapter about the
artifact, is what makes them survive. The reader of the next run is an agent,
and it reads `SKILL.md`.

## Test --- Benchmark the skill

The benchmark is the cycle 1 benchmark plus one new requirement: a colleague
who was not present for cycle 1 must reach the same result.

| Criterion | Result |
|---|---|
| Seeded fixture violation detected | 1 of 1 |
| False positives on the compliant fixture | 0 |
| Cycle 1 metalite finding reproduced | Yes, 3 confirmed sites |
| Coverage statement present | Yes |
| Rules explicitly reported as unchecked | BR-NUM-001.2, BR-NUM-001.3 |
| Approved helper still discarded by hand | Yes, 2 sites per run |

The last row is a deliberate non-improvement. The allowlist was left out of
version 1.0 so that the hardening step has a measured cost to remove rather
than a hypothetical one.

Expected fixture results are recorded in
[`examples/rounding/expected/fixture-findings.md`](https://github.com/elong0527/ai4csr/blob/main/examples/rounding/expected/fixture-findings.md).

## Deploy --- Trigger the skill

::: {.callout-important title="Design, not implementation"}
This section specifies triggers. No scheduled job, CI workflow, or bot has been
committed or run. Treat the table below as a decision to be made with the team
that owns the repository, not as a description of something operating.
:::

The skill can be invoked three ways, and the choice is a governance decision
rather than a technical one.

| Trigger | Runs when | Strength | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **On demand** | A reviewer asks | Zero setup; matches cycle 1 | Depends on someone remembering |
| **On pull request** | Relevant source changes | Catches the violation at the moment it is written | Noise on pull requests that touch no rounding site |
| **Scheduled** | Before release, or every 30 days if any pull request merged since the last run | Catches drift from dependency and helper changes | Findings arrive detached from the change that caused them |

The condition on the scheduled trigger matters more than the interval. A run
against unchanged code produces the same output as the previous run and trains
reviewers to ignore it. Gating on "a pull request merged since the last run"
keeps every run informative.

A workable combination for a Biometrics repository is the pull-request trigger
restricted to paths that can produce reported numbers, plus a release-gate run
that checks the whole source tree.

### Canonical artifact: Release record

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Release model | Advisory. Findings are comments and drafts, never a merge block |
| Versions | Skill v1.0; rule contract BR-NUM-001 v1.0 |
| Permissions | Read the source, run two R scripts, write a draft file |
| Prohibited | Editing source, posting to a repository without explicit approval |
| Accountable reviewer | The rule owner named in the contract |
| Reversal | Remove the skill folder or disable the trigger |

Advisory is the right first release model because the rule contract has never
been enforced before. A check that blocks merges on its first day teaches
people to route around it.

## Maintain --- Harden the skill

The hardening backlog is ordered by measured cost, not by ambition.

**Allowlist of approved wrappers.** The scan reports the organization's own
`round_half_away()` and `fmt_num()` on every run. An allowlist declared in the
rule contract, listing the functions the organization has already approved,
removes the recurring triage. It also creates a governance point worth naming:
adding a function to the allowlist is a policy change, and belongs to the rule
owner rather than to whoever is running the check.

**Run log.** Each run should record the target repository and commit, the rule
contract version, the skill version, the files scanned, every candidate site
with its triage decision and reason, the probe verdicts, and the reviewer's
final classification. Without the discarded sites and their reasons, a later
reviewer cannot tell a deliberate triage from a missed site.

**Coverage as a first-class output.** Version 1.0 states which rules it did not
check. It does not yet state which files it could not parse or which `digits`
arguments it could not resolve. Silence is not evidence.

**Rules 2 and 3.** Rounding stage and display precision were left out because
both need data-flow tracing rather than a line scan. They are the natural
content of a third cycle, and they will shift the balance of the workflow
toward the agent and away from the deterministic scripts, which is a reason to
benchmark them separately.

### The feedback loop is governed

An agent that runs this skill regularly will accumulate good proposals: a
function missing from the catalog, a triage pattern worth writing down, a rule
that is ambiguous in practice. It may propose any of them. The rule owner
approves the change, the contract version increments, and the fixtures gain a
case. An agent does not edit the rule it is checked against.

### Canonical artifact: Monitoring report

There is no operating history to report. The measures this workflow would
monitor are findings and false positives by rule, the human classification mix
of defect, convention, and exception, the triage cost per run, and the number
of runs stopped by an unresolved `digits` argument.

## Summary

The first cycle proved that a rounding rule can be checked. The second cycle
made the check portable: a folder with a description an agent can discover, a
versioned rule contract, two deterministic scripts, an issue template, and an
honest list of what it does not do.

What is real in this chapter is the skill and its measured results on fixtures
and on metalite. What is designed but not built is everything that would make
it run without being asked. That boundary is stated rather than blurred,
because a workflow that has never been triggered automatically has not yet been
tested against the failure mode that matters most: a check that quietly stops
running.
